This notebook expands the fourth unit of the course. The lecture slides are a map; this text is the territory. The unit begins with a data structure — the binary tree, a topic of a first course in algorithms — and ends with one of the most successful learning methods of the last twenty-five years, the random forest. The two halves belong together: a decision tree is a binary tree whose internal nodes ask questions about features and whose leaves hold predictions, and a random forest is a collection of such trees grown on randomised data and averaged. What Sections 2–5 establish about depth, height, traversal and balance is used literally in Sections 6–8, on the breast-cancer data that recurs throughout the course. Every figure and number in the text is produced by code you can see and change.

Learning objectives

  • Define a binary tree recursively; use root, leaf, depth, height and degree correctly; count the nodes of a perfect tree of height $h$.
  • Implement a binary tree as linked nodes, as an array ($2i+1$ / $2i+2$ rule) and as nested dictionaries, and implement the four traversals.
  • State the binary-search-tree invariant, insert and search in $O(h)$, and explain why insertion order determines the height.
  • Explain why balance matters, what a rotation does, and what AVL, red–black and B-trees guarantee.
  • Describe a decision tree as a binary tree over feature space; derive the Gini, entropy and misclassification impurities; find the best split of a feature by hand and with scikit-learn.
  • Diagnose overfitting with depth and pruning curves; read a tree's rules and feature importances with the appropriate caveats.
  • Explain bagging, random feature subsets and the out-of-bag estimate; compare a random forest with a single tree and with the methods of Unit 3 under the methodology of Supplement S1.

1. Why a course on artificial intelligence teaches a data structure

A tree is the natural representation of a hierarchical decision. A clinician triaging chest pain asks a first question (is the electrocardiogram abnormal?), the answer determines the next, and so on until a decision is reached. Written down, the protocol is a tree: each question a node, each answer a branch, each decision a leaf. The first computer-derived protocol of that kind, built in 1982 from 482 emergency-room patients by the recursive-partitioning method this unit calls CART, reduced unnecessary coronary-care admissions without missing more infarctions than physicians did.[27]

The same structure appears throughout computer science for a different reason: a tree that halves the remaining possibilities at every node reaches any of $n$ items in about $\log_2 n$ steps — twenty steps for a million records. Knuth's treatment of trees and searching remains the reference for the vocabulary and the analysis.[1],[2] The unit proceeds in three steps (Figure 1): the binary tree as a data structure (Sections 2–5); the decision tree (Section 6), a binary tree whose nodes — thresholds on features — are learned from data and whose depth controls how much it memorises; and the random forest (Section 7), hundreds of decision trees grown on random resamples of the patients and random subsets of the features, voting together.

The thread of the unit

Every property of a binary tree in Sections 2–5 has a consequence for learning. Height is the number of questions asked before a prediction and, in a learned tree, the main control of overfitting. Balance decides whether a prediction costs logarithmic or linear time. Traversal is how a tree is printed as rules, and how scikit-learn stores it: as arrays indexed by node, the array representation of Section 2.3.

Figure 1. The three objects of the unit: an abstract binary tree (the running example of Section 2); a decision tree over breast-cancer features — the same shape, with a yes/no question at each internal node and a diagnosis at each leaf; and a forest of trees whose votes are combined.

2. Binary trees

2.1 Definitions

A tree is a set of nodes connected by edges with exactly one path between any two nodes; a rooted tree distinguishes one node, the root, from which every other node is reached by going "down". The vocabulary, largely due to Knuth, mixes genealogy and botany:[1]

Term Definition In Figure 1 (left)
Root The unique node with no parent A
Parent / child The node immediately above / below along an edge B is the parent of D and E
Leaf A node with no children D, E, F, G
Internal node A node with at least one child A, B, C
Degree of a node Its number of children 2 for every internal node
Depth of a node Edges from the root; the root has depth 0 depth(D) = 2
Height of a node Edges on the longest path down to a leaf; a leaf has height 0 height(B) = 1
Height of the tree Height of the root = maximum depth 2
Subtree rooted at $v$ $v$ and all its descendants {B, D, E}

A binary tree is a rooted tree in which every node has at most two children, distinguished as left and right. It is full if every node has 0 or 2 children, perfect if it is full and all leaves have the same depth (Figure 1, left), and complete if every level but the last is full and the last is filled from the left — the shape of heaps and of the array representation below.

Height is counted in edges; the empty tree has height −1

Some textbooks count nodes rather than edges, so a single node has height 1 instead of 0. This notebook, scikit-learn (tree.get_depth()) and most algorithm texts count edges and give the empty tree height −1, so that the recursive formula below holds without exceptions. An off-by-one turns $2^{h+1}-1$ into $2^h-1$.

2.2 The recursive definition

A binary tree is either empty, or a root node together with two binary trees, its left and right subtrees. Every algorithm on trees follows this shape — handle the root, recurse left, recurse right — and every property is proved by induction on the height. For instance

$$h(T) = \begin{cases} -1 & T \text{ empty} \\ 1 + \max\big(h(T_\text{left}), h(T_\text{right})\big) & \text{otherwise,} \end{cases}$$ and $n(T) = 0$ for the empty tree, $1 + n(T_\text{left}) + n(T_\text{right})$ otherwise.

2.3 Three representations

The first representation is linked nodes: each node is an object with a value and two references, left and right, None when a child is absent. The cell builds the tree of Figure 1 this way and computes its height and size with the recursive definitions.

# Representation 1: linked nodes. A Node holds a value and references to its left and right children.
class Node:
    '''A node of a binary tree. Children default to None (the empty tree).'''
    def __init__(self, value, left=None, right=None):
        self.value, self.left, self.right = value, left, right
    def __repr__(self):
        return f"Node({self.value!r})"

def height(t):
    '''Height in edges; the empty tree has height -1 (the recursive definition of Section 2.2).'''
    return -1 if t is None else 1 + max(height(t.left), height(t.right))

def count(t):
    return 0 if t is None else 1 + count(t.left) + count(t.right)

def leaves(t):
    if t is None: return []
    if t.left is None and t.right is None: return [t.value]
    return leaves(t.left) + leaves(t.right)

# The seven-node tree of Figure 1 (left), built bottom-up: leaves first, then their parents, then the root.
T = Node("A", Node("B", Node("D"), Node("E")), Node("C", Node("F"), Node("G")))
print("root:", T, "| left child of root:", T.left, "| right child of B:", T.left.right)
print("height:", height(T), "| nodes:", count(T), "| leaves:", leaves(T))
print("height of the subtree at B:", height(T.left), "| height of a leaf:", height(T.left.left), "| of the empty tree:", height(None))

root: Node('A') | left child of root: Node('B') | right child of B: Node('E')
height: 2 | nodes: 7 | leaves: ['D', 'E', 'F', 'G']
height of the subtree at B: 1 | height of a leaf: 0 | of the empty tree: -1

The functions are the recursive definition as code, and the outputs confirm the hand count: height 2, seven nodes, four leaves, height(leaf) = 0, height(empty) = −1.

The second representation is an array: number the nodes level by level, root at 0; the children of node $i$ are at $2i+1$ and $2i+2$ and its parent at $\lfloor (i-1)/2 \rfloor$. No pointers are stored — the shape is in the arithmetic. It is compact for complete trees (the binary heap is exactly this[2]) and wasteful otherwise, because missing nodes still occupy slots. The third is a nested dictionary, convenient for serialising to JSON.

# Representation 2: array (level order, children of i at 2i+1 and 2i+2). Representation 3: nested dictionaries.
def to_array(t, i=0, arr=None):
    '''Fill a level-order array from a linked tree; absent nodes stay None.'''
    if arr is None: arr = [None] * (2 ** (height(t) + 1) - 1)
    if t is not None:
        arr[i] = t.value
        to_array(t.left, 2 * i + 1, arr); to_array(t.right, 2 * i + 2, arr)
    return arr

def to_dict(t):
    return None if t is None else {"value": t.value, "left": to_dict(t.left), "right": to_dict(t.right)}

arr = to_array(T)
print("array:", arr)
for i in range(3):
    print(f"  node {arr[i]} at index {i}: children at {2*i+1} ({arr[2*i+1]}) and {2*i+2} ({arr[2*i+2]})", end="")
    print(f"; parent of index {2*i+1} is {(2*i+1-1)//2} ({arr[(2*i+1-1)//2]})")
print("nested dict:", to_dict(T))

array: ['A', 'B', 'C', 'D', 'E', 'F', 'G']
  node A at index 0: children at 1 (B) and 2 (C); parent of index 1 is 0 (A)
  node B at index 1: children at 3 (D) and 4 (E); parent of index 3 is 1 (B)
  node C at index 2: children at 5 (F) and 6 (G); parent of index 5 is 2 (C)
nested dict: {'value': 'A', 'left': {'value': 'B', 'left': {'value': 'D', 'left': None, 'right': None}, 'right': {'value': 'E', 'left': None, 'right': None}}, 'right': {'value': 'C', 'left': {'value': 'F', 'left': None, 'right': None}, 'right': {'value': 'G', 'left': None, 'right': None}}}

The array reads A B C D E F G, the level-order listing, and the arithmetic recovers every parent–child relation. Section 6.1 shows that scikit-learn stores a learned tree in this spirit — arrays children_left, children_right, feature, threshold indexed by node — with child indices stored explicitly so that unbalanced trees waste no space.

2.4 Traversals

To traverse a tree is to visit every node once in a defined order. The recursive definition offers three places to visit the root — before, between or after the recursive calls — plus one breadth-first order:[1]

Traversal Order Typical use
Pre-order root, left, right printing a tree as nested rules (export_text, Section 6)
In-order left, root, right on a search tree, yields the keys in sorted order (Section 3)
Post-order left, right, root deleting a tree (children first); evaluating expression trees
Level-order depth 0, then depth 1, … the array representation

By hand on Figure 1: pre-order visits A, then B's subtree (B, D, E), then C's: A B D E C F G; in-order D B E A F C G; post-order D E B F G C A; level-order A B C D E F G.

# The four traversals of Section 2.4. The three depth-first ones differ only in WHERE the root is visited.
from collections import deque

def preorder(t):   return [] if t is None else [t.value] + preorder(t.left) + preorder(t.right)
def inorder(t):    return [] if t is None else inorder(t.left) + [t.value] + inorder(t.right)
def postorder(t):  return [] if t is None else postorder(t.left) + postorder(t.right) + [t.value]

def levelorder(t):
    '''Breadth-first: a queue holds the nodes discovered but not yet visited.'''
    out, q = [], deque([t] if t else [])
    while q:
        node = q.popleft(); out.append(node.value)
        if node.left:  q.append(node.left)
        if node.right: q.append(node.right)
    return out

for name, f in [("pre-order", preorder), ("in-order", inorder), ("post-order", postorder), ("level-order", levelorder)]:
    print(f"{name:12s} {' '.join(f(T))}")

pre-order    A B D E C F G
in-order     D B E A F C G
post-order   D E B F G C A
level-order  A B C D E F G

All four match the hand trace, and only the position of [t.value] separates the three depth-first traversals. In-order is the important one: on a search tree it yields the sorted keys.

2.5 Counting nodes

A perfect tree of height $h$ has $2^d$ nodes at depth $d$, so

$$n = \sum_{d=0}^{h} 2^d = 2^{h+1} - 1, \qquad h = \log_2(n+1) - 1,$$ with $2^h$ leaves. Conversely, any binary tree with $n$ nodes has height at least $\lceil \log_2(n+1) \rceil - 1$ and at most $n-1$ (a chain). These two bounds, logarithmic and linear, are the whole story of Sections 3 and 4.
# Perfect binary trees of height 0..6: count nodes and leaves and compare with 2^(h+1) - 1 and 2^h.
def perfect(h, label=1):
    '''Build a perfect binary tree of height h with consecutive integer labels in level order.'''
    if h < 0: return None
    return Node(label, perfect(h - 1, 2 * label), perfect(h - 1, 2 * label + 1))

rows = []
for h in range(7):
    t = perfect(h)
    rows.append({"height h": h, "nodes": count(t), "2^(h+1)-1": 2 ** (h + 1) - 1,
                 "leaves": len(leaves(t)), "2^h": 2 ** h, "height() recomputed": height(t)})
pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("height h")
nodes 2^(h+1)-1 leaves 2^h height() recomputed
height h
0 1 1 1 1 0
1 3 3 2 2 1
2 7 7 4 4 2
3 15 15 8 8 3
4 31 31 16 16 4
5 63 63 32 32 5
6 127 127 64 64 6

The counts agree with the formula: 1, 3, 7, 15, 31, 63, 127. Read the other way, a perfect tree holding a million items has height only 19, so any question about its contents is answered in about twenty steps — provided the tree stays close to perfect.

Exercise 1

Modify perfect() so that each node has only a right child. How many nodes does a chain of height $h$ have, and how many slots does to_array() waste for a chain of height 4? This is the degenerate shape of Section 3.4.

3. Binary search trees

3.1 The invariant

A binary search tree (BST) holds keys from an ordered set and satisfies, at every node $v$, the BST invariant:

$$\text{every key in the left subtree of } v \;<\; \text{key}(v) \;<\; \text{every key in the right subtree of } v ,$$ a condition on whole subtrees, not only on the two children. Duplicate keys are disallowed here.

To search for $k$: start at the root; stop if $k$ equals the node's key; go left if smaller, right if larger; if the child is absent, $k$ is not in the tree. To insert $k$: search, and attach a new leaf where the search fell off. Each step descends one level, so both operations cost at most the height: $O(h)$. What matters is how large $h$ is relative to $n$.[2] The implementation below counts key comparisons for the cost experiments of Sections 3.4 and 4.5.

# A minimal binary search tree with insertion, search and a comparison counter.
class BST:
    '''Binary search tree on distinct keys; counts key comparisons for the cost experiments.'''
    def __init__(self):
        self.root, self.comparisons = None, 0

    def insert(self, key):
        self.root = self._insert(self.root, key)

    def _insert(self, t, key):
        if t is None: return Node(key)                 # fell off the tree: attach a new leaf here
        self.comparisons += 1
        if key < t.value:   t.left  = self._insert(t.left, key)
        elif key > t.value: t.right = self._insert(t.right, key)
        return t                                       # equal keys are ignored

    def search(self, key):
        '''Return the path of keys visited (last element == key if found).'''
        path, t = [], self.root
        while t is not None:
            path.append(t.value); self.comparisons += 1
            if key == t.value: return path, True
            t = t.left if key < t.value else t.right
        return path, False

    def height(self):  return height(self.root)
    def sorted_keys(self): return inorder(self.root)

bst = BST()
for k in [41, 20, 65, 11, 29, 50, 91, 32, 72, 99]:
    bst.insert(k)
print("in-order traversal:", bst.sorted_keys())
print("height:", bst.height(), "| nodes:", count(bst.root))
for k in [32, 72, 60]:
    path, found = bst.search(k)
    print(f"search {k}: path {path} -> {'found' if found else 'absent'} after {len(path)} comparisons")

in-order traversal: [11, 20, 29, 32, 41, 50, 65, 72, 91, 99]
height: 3 | nodes: 10
search 32: path [41, 20, 29, 32] -> found after 4 comparisons
search 72: path [41, 65, 91, 72] -> found after 4 comparisons
search 60: path [41, 65, 50] -> absent after 3 comparisons

The in-order traversal returns the keys in ascending order although they were inserted in no particular order — the invariant made visible, and the reason tree sort works. The ten keys produced height 3, the minimum $\lceil \log_2 11 \rceil - 1$, and each search stops after at most $h+1 = 4$ comparisons, found or not.

3.2 Why in-order yields sorted keys

By induction on the height: in-order visits the left subtree, the root, then the right subtree; by the invariant every left key is smaller than the root and every right key larger; by the inductive hypothesis each subtree is visited in sorted order; the concatenation is sorted. The same argument gives an $O(n)$ check of the invariant: traverse in-order and verify the sequence increases.

3.3 Deletion, in outline

A leaf is removed; a node with one child is replaced by that child; a node with two children receives the key of its in-order successor (the smallest key of its right subtree), and the successor, which has at most one child, is deleted instead. The invariant is preserved and the cost is $O(h)$. Knuth notes that repeated deletions with this rule slowly unbalance the tree — one motivation for Section 4.[2]

3.4 Degeneration: the height depends on the insertion order

Nothing in the insertion algorithm keeps the tree short. If keys arrive in sorted order each new key goes right: the tree is a chain of height $n-1$ and search is a linear scan dressed as a tree. If keys arrive in random order, the root splits the rest roughly in half, each subtree is again a random BST, and the expected height is proportional to $\log n$.[2] Sorted input is not contrived: patient identifiers, timestamps and accession numbers are generated in increasing order.

# Height of a BST after inserting n keys in sorted order (degenerate) versus random order (20 shuffles per n).
import sys; sys.setrecursionlimit(10_000)                      # the sorted chain is deep: recursion must be allowed to go n levels
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
ns = [10, 20, 50, 100, 200, 500, 1000, 2000]
rows = []
for n in ns:
    sorted_tree = BST()
    for k in range(n): sorted_tree.insert(k)
    random_h = []
    for _ in range(20):
        t = BST()
        for k in rng.permutation(n): t.insert(int(k))
        random_h.append(t.height())
    rows.append({"n": n, "sorted input": sorted_tree.height(), "random input (mean)": np.mean(random_h),
                 "random input (max of 20)": max(random_h), "log2(n)": np.log2(n)})
res = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("n")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.6))
ax.plot(ns, res["sorted input"], "s-", color=ORANGE, label="sorted insertion: h = n - 1")
ax.plot(ns, res["random input (mean)"], "o-", color=BLUE, label="random insertion: mean height of 20 trees")
ax.plot(ns, res["log2(n)"], "--", color=GREY, label="log2(n), the perfect-tree lower bound")
ax.set_xscale("log"); ax.set_yscale("log"); ax.set_xlabel("number of keys n"); ax.set_ylabel("height of the tree")
ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8); ax.set_title("Height of a binary search tree versus number of keys and insertion order")
fig.tight_layout()
res.round(1)
sorted input random input (mean) random input (max of 20) log2(n)

Figure 2. Height of a binary search tree versus number of keys, logarithmic axes. Sorted insertion gives $h = n-1$; random insertion gives heights growing like a constant times $\log_2 n$ — mean height about 24 at $n = 2{,}000$, against 1,999 for the chain. Dashed: the perfect-tree lower bound.

The random trees are two to three times taller than a perfect tree — the price of not controlling the shape — but still logarithmic: some twenty-five comparisons per search at $n = 2{,}000$ where the chain needs up to 2,000. A BST is only as fast as its shape, and the shape is at the mercy of the data unless the algorithm maintains it.

Exercise 2

Insert range(n) after swapping 5 % of adjacent pairs at random: is the height closer to the sorted or the random case? Then insert in "median first, then the medians of the two halves, …" order. What height results, and why is it the minimum possible?

4. Balanced trees

4.1 Why balance matters and what a rotation does

A search tree is balanced when its height is $O(\log n)$ for every sequence of insertions and deletions, and self-balancing when it restores balance after each operation with a small, local amount of work, so that every operation is logarithmic in the worst case rather than on average. The restoring tool is the rotation: a rearrangement of a node and one child that changes the heights of the two sides by one while preserving the in-order sequence, and therefore the invariant. In Figure 3, a right rotation about $y$ with left child $x$ makes $x$ the parent and $y$ its right child, and moves subtree $B$ (keys between $x$ and $y$) from the right of $x$ to the left of $y$, at the cost of a constant number of pointer changes.

Figure 3. A right rotation about $y$: subtree $A$ rises one level, $C$ sinks one, $B$ changes parent, and the in-order sequence $A, x, B, y, C$ is unchanged. The left rotation is the mirror image; a double rotation handles the case in which the heavy subtree is $B$.

4.2 AVL trees

The first self-balancing tree, published in 1962 by Adelson-Velskii and Landis, maintains the AVL condition: at every node the heights of the two subtrees differ by at most one.[3] After an insertion the algorithm walks back up the path updating a stored balance factor; at the first node where it reaches $\pm 2$, one single or double rotation restores the condition. The height is at most about $1.44\log_2(n+2)$, so every operation is $O(\log n)$ in the worst case; Knuth derives the bound via Fibonacci numbers.[2]

4.3 Red–black trees

A red–black tree relaxes the AVL condition in exchange for fewer rotations: each node carries a colour bit, the root is black, a red node has no red child, and every path from a node to the empty leaves below passes the same number of black nodes. No root-to-leaf path is then more than twice as long as any other, so the height is at most $2\log_2(n+1)$. Bayer introduced the structure in 1972 as the symmetric binary B-tree[4] and Guibas and Sedgewick gave it the colour formulation in 1978.[5] It is the usual implementation of ordered maps (C++ std::map, Java TreeMap); Python's dict is a hash table, faster for exact lookup but unable to answer range queries.

4.4 B-trees in databases

On disk the cost that matters is the number of blocks read, and a binary node wastes a block on one key. The B-tree of Bayer and McCreight stores hundreds of keys per node, sized to a disk page, with all leaves at the same depth and all nodes at least half full.[6] With branching factor 500, 125 million keys fit in height 3. Every relational database index uses a B-tree variant; when a hospital system retrieves a record by identifier in milliseconds, it is walking one.

4.5 Experiment: search cost in a degenerate versus a balanced tree

Implementing AVL rebalancing is beyond the unit, but its effect is easy to show: the same keys inserted in sorted order give a chain, and inserted median-first (the solution of Exercise 2) give a perfect tree. The cell inserts 1,023 keys both ways and counts the comparisons of 2,000 random searches.

# Search cost: 1,023 keys inserted as a chain (sorted) versus as a perfect tree (median-first order), 2,000 searches each.
def median_first(keys):
    '''Insertion order that produces a perfect BST from a sorted list: middle, then recurse on both halves.'''
    if not keys: return []
    m = len(keys) // 2
    return [keys[m]] + median_first(keys[:m]) + median_first(keys[m + 1:])

keys = list(range(1023))                                   # 1023 = 2^10 - 1 -> a perfect tree of height 9 is possible
chain, balanced = BST(), BST()
for k in keys:               chain.insert(k)
for k in median_first(keys): balanced.insert(k)

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
queries = rng.integers(0, 1023, 2000)
rows = []
for name, t in [("degenerate (sorted insertion)", chain), ("balanced (median-first insertion)", balanced)]:
    t.comparisons = 0
    for q in queries: t.search(int(q))
    rows.append({"tree": name, "height": t.height(), "comparisons per search (mean)": t.comparisons / len(queries),
                 "worst case (h + 1)": t.height() + 1})
pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("tree").round(1)
height comparisons per search (mean) worst case (h + 1)
tree
degenerate (sorted insertion) 1022 522.6 1023
balanced (median-first insertion) 9 9.0 10

The balanced tree has height 9, the minimum for 1,023 keys, and answers a search in 9 comparisons on average; the chain has height 1,022 and needs about 520 for the same keys. A self-balancing tree pays a small constant per insertion to keep the second column logarithmic. In the second half of the unit the trees are shaped by data and depth limits rather than by rotations, but the cost of a prediction is still the depth of the leaf reached, and a deep tree is still a slow and — as we shall see — an over-specific one.

Bridge to bioinformatics

A suffix tree indexes a genome so that any substring is found in time proportional to its length; the k-d tree and ball tree speed up the nearest-neighbour search of Unit 3 (scikit-learn's KNeighborsClassifier uses one by default); the phylogenetic tree of UPGMA or neighbour-joining is a binary tree whose post-order traversal computes ancestral states; the clustering dendrogram of Unit 5 is a binary tree built from the leaves up.

5. Worked example by hand: building a search tree

Insert 50, 30, 70, 20, 40, 60, 80, in this order, into an empty BST ("smaller goes left, larger goes right"):

Step Key Comparisons Placement
1 50 — root
2 30 30 < 50 → left left child of 50
3 70 70 > 50 → right right child of 50
4 20 20 < 50 → left; 20 < 30 → left left child of 30
5 40 40 < 50 → left; 40 > 30 → right right child of 30
6 60 60 > 50 → right; 60 < 70 → left left child of 70
7 80 80 > 50 → right; 80 > 70 → right right child of 70 
            50
          /    \
        30      70
       /  \    /  \
     20   40  60   80

The tree has 7 nodes and height 2 and is perfect — this order is the median-first order of Section 4.5. Its traversals: pre-order 50, 30, 20, 40, 70, 60, 80; in-order 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80 (sorted, as the invariant requires); post-order 20, 40, 30, 60, 80, 70, 50; level-order 50, 30, 70, 20, 40, 60, 80. Searching for 60 follows 50 → 70 → 60 (three comparisons); searching for 65 follows the same path, finds no right child of 60, and reports absence after three comparisons. The same keys inserted in sorted order give a chain of height 6 in which the search for 80 takes seven comparisons. The cell confirms every statement and draws both trees.

# Confirming the hand-worked example of Section 5 in code.
hand = BST()
for k in [50, 30, 70, 20, 40, 60, 80]:
    hand.insert(k)
print("nodes:", count(hand.root), "| height:", hand.height(), "| leaves:", leaves(hand.root))
for name, f in [("pre-order", preorder), ("in-order", inorder), ("post-order", postorder), ("level-order", levelorder)]:
    print(f"{name:12s} {f(hand.root)}")
for q in [60, 65]:
    path, found = hand.search(q)
    print(f"search {q}: path {path} -> {'found' if found else 'absent'} ({len(path)} comparisons)")
chain7 = BST()
for k in sorted([50, 30, 70, 20, 40, 60, 80]): chain7.insert(k)
print("same keys inserted in sorted order -> height", chain7.height(), "| search 80 takes", len(chain7.search(80)[0]), "comparisons")

# The tree drawn from the data structure itself (positions from the in-order index and the depth).
def draw_bst(t, ax):
    order = inorder(t); pos = {}
    def place(node, depth):
        if node is None: return
        pos[node.value] = (order.index(node.value), -depth); place(node.left, depth + 1); place(node.right, depth + 1)
        for ch in (node.left, node.right):
            if ch: ax.plot([pos[node.value][0], order.index(ch.value)], [-depth, -depth - 1], color=GREY, lw=1, zorder=1)
    place(t, 0)
    for k, (x, y) in pos.items():
        ax.text(x, y, str(k), ha="center", va="center", fontsize=9, bbox=dict(boxstyle="circle,pad=0.3", fc="#dfe7f1", ec="k"), zorder=3)
    ax.axis("off")
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 2.8), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1.2, 1]})
draw_bst(hand.root, axes[0]); axes[0].set_title("keys inserted 50, 30, 70, 20, 40, 60, 80 (height 2)")
draw_bst(chain7.root, axes[1]); axes[1].set_title("same keys inserted in sorted order (height 6)")
fig.tight_layout()

nodes: 7 | height: 2 | leaves: [20, 40, 60, 80]
pre-order    [50, 30, 20, 40, 70, 60, 80]
in-order     [20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80]
post-order   [20, 40, 30, 60, 80, 70, 50]
level-order  [50, 30, 70, 20, 40, 60, 80]
search 60: path [50, 70, 60] -> found (3 comparisons)
search 65: path [50, 70, 60] -> absent (3 comparisons)
same keys inserted in sorted order -> height 6 | search 80 takes 7 comparisons

Figure 4. The two trees of the worked example, drawn from the data structure: horizontal position is the in-order rank, vertical position the depth. Same keys, same in-order sequence, heights 2 and 6.

The code reproduces the hand trace exactly; you should be able to perform it for any short list of keys on paper.

6. From binary trees to decision trees

6.1 A decision tree is a binary tree over feature space

Return to the Wisconsin breast-cancer data: 569 fine-needle aspirates, 30 features computed from images of the cell nuclei, labelled malignant (212) or benign (357) by biopsy.[28] A decision tree classifier is a binary tree in which every internal node holds a test "is feature $j$ ≤ threshold $t$?", the left child is taken when the answer is yes, and every leaf holds a class. Classifying a patient is a search in the sense of Section 3, driven by the patient's features, in which the path itself is the answer. Geometrically each test is a hyperplane perpendicular to one axis, so the leaves partition feature space into axis-aligned boxes. The cell fits a depth-2 tree to the training part of a stratified 70/30 split (used for the rest of the unit, following Supplement S1), draws it, and inspects scikit-learn's internal representation.

# A depth-2 decision tree on the breast-cancer data, and its internal array representation.
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier, plot_tree, export_text

cancer = datasets.load_breast_cancer(as_frame=True)
X, y = cancer.data, cancer.target                     # y: 0 = malignant, 1 = benign (scikit-learn's coding)
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.3, random_state=0, stratify=y)
print(f"training cases {len(X_tr)}, test cases {len(X_te)}; classes {dict(enumerate(cancer.target_names))}")

tree2 = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=2, random_state=0).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9.5, 3.6))
plot_tree(tree2, feature_names=list(X.columns), class_names=list(cancer.target_names), filled=True, impurity=True,
          proportion=False, rounded=True, fontsize=8, ax=ax)
ax.set_title("A learned decision tree of depth 2 (training part of the breast-cancer data)")
fig.tight_layout()

s = tree2.tree_
print("nodes:", s.node_count, "| depth:", tree2.get_depth(), "| leaves:", tree2.get_n_leaves())
print("children_left :", s.children_left, "   (-1 marks a leaf)")
print("children_right:", s.children_right)
print("feature index :", s.feature, "   threshold:", s.threshold.round(3))

training cases 398, test cases 171; classes {0: np.str_('malignant'), 1: np.str_('benign')}
nodes: 7 | depth: 2 | leaves: 4
children_left : [ 1  2 -1 -1  5 -1 -1]    (-1 marks a leaf)
children_right: [ 4  3 -1 -1  6 -1 -1]
feature index : [22 27 -2 -2 27 -2 -2]    threshold: [106.1     0.158  -2.     -2.      0.142  -2.     -2.   ]

Figure 5. A depth-2 tree learned from 398 training cases. Each box shows the test (absent in leaves), the Gini impurity, the number of training cases reaching the node, their class counts [malignant, benign] and the majority class, which is the prediction. A root-to-leaf path is a rule.

The printed arrays prove the claim that opened the section: scikit-learn stores the tree as parallel arrays indexed by node, with −1 marking a leaf. The tree has 7 nodes, the perfect-tree count of Section 2.5, numbered in pre-order — which is why the root's right child is node 4, after the whole left subtree. Everything plot_tree and export_text print is a traversal of these arrays.

6.2 Impurity: how good is a split?

Learning a tree means choosing the tests. The idea common to the two traditions that invented the method — the statistical CART of Breiman, Friedman, Olshen and Stone[7] and Quinlan's ID3 and C4.5[8],[9] — is that a good test sends the two classes to different sides. The impurity of a node makes this numerical: 0 when all cases share one class, largest when the classes are equally mixed. For class proportions $p_1, \dots, p_K$:

$$\text{Gini: } G = 1 - \sum_k p_k^2, \qquad \text{Entropy: } H = -\sum_k p_k \log_2 p_k, \qquad \text{Misclassification: } E = 1 - \max_k p_k .$$ Gini is the probability that two cases drawn from the node belong to different classes (CART's default); entropy is the expected number of bits to encode a case's class (ID3); misclassification is the error of the majority prediction. For two classes, $G = 2p(1-p)$, $H = -p\log_2 p - (1-p)\log_2(1-p)$, $E = \min(p, 1-p)$.

The quality of a split is the decrease in impurity, weighted by the number of cases on each side:

$$\Delta I = I - \left( \frac{n_L}{n} I_L + \frac{n_R}{n} I_R \right),$$ called the information gain when $I$ is the entropy. The chosen split maximises $\Delta I$.
# The three impurity measures for a two-class node as a function of the proportion p of one class.
p = np.linspace(0.001, 0.999, 400)
gini = 2 * p * (1 - p)
entropy = -(p * np.log2(p) + (1 - p) * np.log2(1 - p))
miscl = np.minimum(p, 1 - p)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.2, 3.6))
ax.plot(p, entropy, color=BLUE, label="entropy  H = -p log2 p - (1-p) log2 (1-p)")
ax.plot(p, gini, color=ORANGE, label="Gini  G = 2 p (1-p)")
ax.plot(p, miscl, color=GREEN, label="misclassification  E = min(p, 1-p)")
ax.plot(p, entropy / 2, ":", color=BLUE, lw=1, label="entropy / 2 (for shape comparison)")
ax.set_xlabel("proportion p of one class at the node"); ax.set_ylabel("impurity"); ax.set_ylim(0, 1.05)
ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8); ax.set_title("Impurity of a two-class node")
fig.tight_layout()
print(f"at p = 0.5: Gini {2*0.25:.3f}, entropy {1.0:.3f}, misclassification {0.5:.3f}")
print(f"at p = 0.9: Gini {2*0.9*0.1:.3f}, entropy {-(0.9*np.log2(0.9)+0.1*np.log2(0.1)):.3f}, misclassification {0.1:.3f}")

at p = 0.5: Gini 0.500, entropy 1.000, misclassification 0.500
at p = 0.9: Gini 0.180, entropy 0.469, misclassification 0.100

Figure 6. The three impurity measures for a two-class node: all vanish for a pure node and peak at $p = 0.5$. Gini and entropy are strictly concave and nearly the same shape (dotted: entropy rescaled); misclassification is piecewise linear.

The shape matters more than the values. Because Gini and entropy are strictly concave, any split that makes the children less mixed decreases them even if no child changes its majority class; the misclassification error can stay unchanged under a useful split when both children keep the parent's majority class (a 60 : 40 parent split into 30 : 10 and 30 : 30 keeps $E = 0.4 \times 0.25 + 0.6 \times 0.5 = 0.40$, the parent's value, while Gini falls from 0.48 to $0.4 \times 0.375 + 0.6 \times 0.5 = 0.45$). CART and C4.5 therefore grow with Gini or entropy and use the misclassification error only to evaluate the finished tree.[7],[23]

6.3 The greedy recursive algorithm, with a split computed by hand

CART grows a classification tree as follows:

  1. Start with all training cases at the root.
  2. For every feature $j$ and every threshold $t$ between consecutive sorted values of $x_j$ at the node, compute $\Delta I$ for the split "$x_j \le t$".
  3. Take the split with the largest $\Delta I$ and send the cases to two children.
  4. Recurse on each child until a stopping rule is met: pure node, too few cases, maximum depth, or no split decreases impurity.
  5. Label each leaf with its majority class (or its class proportions).

The algorithm is greedy: it chooses the best split now and never revisits it. It need not find the smallest or most accurate tree — finding an optimal tree is NP-complete[10] — but one level costs only $O(p\, n \log n)$.

By hand. Ten patients, five malignant (M) and five benign (B); test "worst radius ≤ 16.8": six satisfy it (5 B, 1 M), four do not (4 M).

  • Parent: $G = 1 - (0.5^2 + 0.5^2) = 0.5$; $H = 1$ bit.
  • Left (5 B, 1 M): $G_L = 1 - (5/6)^2 - (1/6)^2 = 10/36 \approx 0.278$; $H_L = -\tfrac56\log_2\tfrac56 - \tfrac16\log_2\tfrac16 \approx 0.650$ bits.
  • Right (4 M): $G_R = H_R = 0$.
  • Weighted children: $0.6 \times 0.278 = 0.167$; $0.6 \times 0.650 = 0.390$ bits.
  • Decrease: $\Delta G = 0.333$; information gain $0.610$ bits.

A competing test sending 3 B + 2 M left and 2 B + 3 M right gives $G_L = G_R = 0.48$ and $\Delta G = 0.02$. The cell confirms the arithmetic.

# Impurity functions and the hand-worked split of Section 6.3.
def gini_index(labels):
    '''Gini impurity of a vector of class labels.'''
    _, counts = np.unique(labels, return_counts=True); pk = counts / counts.sum()
    return 1 - np.sum(pk ** 2)

def entropy_bits(labels):
    _, counts = np.unique(labels, return_counts=True); pk = counts / counts.sum()
    return -np.sum(pk * np.log2(pk))

def split_quality(y_left, y_right, impurity=gini_index):
    '''Decrease in impurity (information gain when impurity=entropy_bits) of splitting a node into two children.'''
    y_all = np.concatenate([y_left, y_right]); n, nL = len(y_all), len(y_left)
    children = (nL / n) * impurity(y_left) + ((n - nL) / n) * impurity(y_right)
    return impurity(y_all) - children, children

left, right = np.array(list("BBBBBM")), np.array(list("MMMM"))         # the hand example: 5B+1M left, 4M right
dG, childG = split_quality(left, right, gini_index)
dH, childH = split_quality(left, right, entropy_bits)
print(f"parent Gini {gini_index(np.r_[left, right]):.3f}; left Gini {gini_index(left):.3f}; right Gini {gini_index(right):.3f}")
print(f"weighted child Gini {childG:.3f} -> decrease {dG:.3f}")
print(f"parent entropy {entropy_bits(np.r_[left, right]):.3f} bits; left {entropy_bits(left):.3f}; weighted child {childH:.3f} -> information gain {dH:.3f} bits")
dG2, _ = split_quality(np.array(list("BBBMM")), np.array(list("BBMMM")), gini_index)
print(f"competing split (3B+2M | 2B+3M): decrease in Gini {dG2:.3f}")

parent Gini 0.500; left Gini 0.278; right Gini 0.000
weighted child Gini 0.167 -> decrease 0.333
parent entropy 1.000 bits; left 0.650; weighted child 0.390 -> information gain 0.610 bits
competing split (3B+2M | 2B+3M): decrease in Gini 0.020

Every number of the hand calculation is reproduced. This procedure — child impurities, weighted by size, subtracted from the parent — is the entire inner loop of CART.

6.4 One split of a real feature, by exhaustive search and by scikit-learn

Step 2, for a continuous feature, is a scan: sort the values at the node, take the midpoint between consecutive distinct values as candidate thresholds, and compute the weighted child impurity for each. The cell scans worst radius over the 398 training cases, then asks DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=1) — a decision stump — to do the same, on that feature alone and then with all 30 features.

# Exhaustive scan of the thresholds of 'worst radius' (the inner loop of CART), then confirmation with a depth-1 tree.
feat = "worst radius"
x_f, y_arr = X_tr[feat].to_numpy(), y_tr.to_numpy()
values = np.sort(np.unique(x_f)); candidates = (values[:-1] + values[1:]) / 2      # midpoints between consecutive values
weighted = np.array([split_quality(y_arr[x_f <= t], y_arr[x_f > t])[1] for t in candidates])
best = candidates[weighted.argmin()]
print(f"{len(candidates)} candidate thresholds scanned; parent Gini {gini_index(y_arr):.4f}")
print(f"best threshold {feat} <= {best:.3f}: weighted child Gini {weighted.min():.4f}, decrease {gini_index(y_arr) - weighted.min():.4f}")
print(f"  left: {np.sum(x_f <= best)} cases ({np.sum((x_f <= best) & (y_arr == 0))} malignant), right: {np.sum(x_f > best)} cases ({np.sum((x_f > best) & (y_arr == 0))} malignant)")

stump_1 = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=1, random_state=0).fit(X_tr[[feat]], y_tr)
stump_30 = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=1, random_state=0).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
print(f"sklearn stump on '{feat}' only : threshold {stump_1.tree_.threshold[0]:.3f}; test accuracy {stump_1.score(X_te[[feat]], y_te):.3f}")
print(f"sklearn stump on all 30 features: splits on '{X.columns[stump_30.tree_.feature[0]]}' <= {stump_30.tree_.threshold[0]:.3f}; "
      f"test accuracy {stump_30.score(X_te, y_te):.3f}")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.3))
ax.plot(candidates, weighted, color=BLUE, lw=1.2)
ax.axvline(best, color=ORANGE, ls="--", lw=1); ax.plot(best, weighted.min(), "o", color=ORANGE)
ax.annotate(f"best split: {best:.2f}", (best, weighted.min()), xytext=(best + 2, weighted.min() + 0.03), fontsize=8)
ax.set_xlabel(f"candidate threshold on '{feat}'"); ax.set_ylabel("weighted Gini of the two children")
ax.set_title("Scanning every candidate threshold of one feature (the inner loop of CART)")
fig.tight_layout()

340 candidate thresholds scanned; parent Gini 0.4672
best threshold worst radius <= 16.805: weighted child Gini 0.1307, decrease 0.3365
  left: 262 cases (20 malignant), right: 136 cases (128 malignant)
sklearn stump on 'worst radius' only : threshold 16.805; test accuracy 0.906
sklearn stump on all 30 features: splits on 'worst perimeter' <= 106.100; test accuracy 0.889

Figure 7. Weighted Gini of the two children as a function of the threshold on worst radius, over 340 candidate midpoints. The minimum is at about 16.8: tumours whose largest nuclear radius exceeds it are overwhelmingly malignant (128 of 136 training cases).

The scan finds the threshold 16.805 with weighted Gini 0.131, down from 0.467, and scikit-learn's stump on the same feature finds exactly the same threshold — its algorithm is the scan just written. Given all 30 features the stump prefers worst perimeter, with a slightly larger decrease: perimeter and radius are nearly the same measurement, and which wins is a matter of a few training cases, a first sign of the instability of Section 6.10. A single question already classifies about 90 % of the test cases.

Why only midpoints — and why trees need no scaling

Any threshold strictly between two consecutive sorted values gives the same split, so one representative per gap suffices. It follows that a tree is invariant to any monotone transformation of a feature: logarithms, standardisation or a change of units alter the thresholds' values but not the splits. This is why trees need no feature scaling, unlike k-NN and SVM in Unit 3.

6.5 Growing the full tree and reading its rules

Left to run until every leaf is pure, the algorithm classifies every training case correctly. The cell grows that tree, reports its size and accuracies, and prints and draws a depth-3 tree.

# The unpruned tree: perfect on training data, worse on test data. Rules printed as a pre-order traversal.
full = DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=0).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
print(f"unpruned tree: depth {full.get_depth()}, {full.get_n_leaves()} leaves, {full.tree_.node_count} nodes")
print(f"  accuracy on training cases {full.score(X_tr, y_tr):.3f} | on the {len(y_te)} test cases {full.score(X_te, y_te):.3f}")
tree3 = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=3, random_state=0).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
print(f"depth-3 tree: {tree3.get_n_leaves()} leaves; training accuracy {tree3.score(X_tr, y_tr):.3f}, test accuracy {tree3.score(X_te, y_te):.3f}\n")
print(export_text(tree3, feature_names=list(X.columns), class_names=["malignant", "benign"], decimals=2, show_weights=True))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9.5, 4.2))
plot_tree(tree3, feature_names=list(X.columns), class_names=list(cancer.target_names), filled=True, impurity=False,
          rounded=True, fontsize=7, ax=ax)
ax.set_title("The same depth-3 tree drawn; each leaf is an axis-aligned box in the 30-dimensional feature space")
fig.tight_layout()

Figure 8. The depth-3 tree printed above as text, drawn. Any root-to-leaf path is an IF–THEN rule: the first question concerns the size of the largest nuclei, the next ones their contour (concave points) or texture. Leaves reached by one or two training cases are the ones most likely to encode noise.

The unpruned tree reaches 100 % training accuracy, as it must, with 16 leaves and depth 6; on the 171 test cases it is correct in 90.6 %. The depth-3 tree, with half the leaves, differs from it by one test case: the extra splits learned the accidents of the 398 training cases, not the pattern. This is overfitting, the theme of Supplement S1, and depth is the knob that controls it. The export_text output is a pre-order traversal in which indentation encodes depth and weights are the class counts at each leaf.

6.6 Depth versus overfitting

The experiment grows trees of maximum depth 1 to 12 and records the training accuracy, the 5-fold stratified cross-validated accuracy within the training part (the honest estimate of S1), and the test accuracy — shown for illustration only, never used to choose the depth.

# Training, cross-validated and test accuracy as a function of the maximum depth of the tree.
from sklearn.model_selection import StratifiedKFold, cross_val_score
cv5 = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=0)
depths = range(1, 13)
rows = []
for d in depths:
    t = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=d, random_state=0)
    cv_acc = cross_val_score(t, X_tr, y_tr, cv=cv5)
    t.fit(X_tr, y_tr)
    rows.append({"max_depth": d, "train": t.score(X_tr, y_tr), "cv (5-fold, training part)": cv_acc.mean(),
                 "cv std": cv_acc.std(), "test (illustration only)": t.score(X_te, y_te), "leaves": t.get_n_leaves()})
curve = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("max_depth")
best_d = curve["cv (5-fold, training part)"].idxmax()
print("depth with the best cross-validated accuracy:", best_d)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.6))
ax.plot(depths, curve["train"], "o-", color=GREY, label="training accuracy")
ax.errorbar(depths, curve["cv (5-fold, training part)"], yerr=curve["cv std"], fmt="s-", color=BLUE, capsize=2, label="5-fold CV accuracy (training part)")
ax.plot(depths, curve["test (illustration only)"], "^--", color=ORANGE, label="test accuracy (not used for selection)")
ax.axvline(best_d, color=BLUE, ls=":", lw=1)
ax.set_xlabel("maximum depth of the tree"); ax.set_ylabel("accuracy"); ax.set_ylim(0.85, 1.01)
ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8, loc="lower right"); ax.set_title("Depth controls overfitting")
fig.tight_layout()
curve.round(3)

Beyond a certain complexity, capacity buys training accuracy and nothing else. The cross-validated optimum is depth 4 (0.927), but the standard deviation across folds is two to three points, so the honest statement is "a depth of about 2 to 5 is as good as any".

6.7 Cost-complexity pruning

A depth limit cuts every branch at the same level, although some deserve to be deeper. CART's cost-complexity pruning grows the full tree and then removes the branches that contribute least to the fit relative to their size: for a tree $T$ with $|T|$ leaves and training error $R(T)$,

$$R_\alpha(T) = R(T) + \alpha\,|T| ,$$ where $\alpha \ge 0$ is the price of a leaf. As $\alpha$ grows the optimal subtree loses its weakest branches one by one; the optimal subtrees are nested, so the whole sequence is cheap to compute, and $\alpha$ is chosen by cross-validation.[7],[23]
# The cost-complexity pruning path: effective alphas, tree sizes and cross-validated accuracy along the path.
path = full.cost_complexity_pruning_path(X_tr, y_tr)
alphas = path.ccp_alphas[:-1]                                   # the last alpha leaves only the root; skip it
rows = []
for a in alphas:
    t = DecisionTreeClassifier(ccp_alpha=a, random_state=0)
    acc = cross_val_score(t, X_tr, y_tr, cv=cv5)
    t.fit(X_tr, y_tr)
    rows.append({"ccp_alpha": a, "leaves": t.get_n_leaves(), "depth": t.get_depth(), "cv accuracy": acc.mean(), "cv std": acc.std(),
                 "test accuracy": t.score(X_te, y_te)})
prune = pd.DataFrame(rows)
best = prune.loc[prune["cv accuracy"].idxmax()]
pruned = DecisionTreeClassifier(ccp_alpha=best["ccp_alpha"], random_state=0).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
print(f"{len(alphas)} subtrees on the path. Best cross-validated alpha = {best['ccp_alpha']:.4f}: "
      f"{int(best['leaves'])} leaves, depth {int(best['depth'])}, CV accuracy {best['cv accuracy']:.3f}, test accuracy {best['test accuracy']:.3f}")

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.5, 3.4))
axes[0].step(prune["ccp_alpha"], prune["leaves"], where="post", color=BLUE); axes[0].set_xlabel("ccp_alpha"); axes[0].set_ylabel("number of leaves")
axes[0].set_title("Pruning collapses leaves as alpha grows")
axes[1].errorbar(prune["ccp_alpha"], prune["cv accuracy"], yerr=prune["cv std"], fmt="o-", color=BLUE, capsize=2, label="5-fold CV accuracy")
axes[1].plot(prune["ccp_alpha"], prune["test accuracy"], "^--", color=ORANGE, label="test accuracy (illustration)")
axes[1].axvline(best["ccp_alpha"], color=GREY, ls=":"); axes[1].set_xlabel("ccp_alpha"); axes[1].set_ylabel("accuracy")
axes[1].legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8); axes[1].set_title("Accuracy along the pruning path")
fig.tight_layout()

11 subtrees on the path. Best cross-validated alpha = 0.0196: 4 leaves, depth 3, CV accuracy 0.925, test accuracy 0.901

Figure 10. Left: leaves of the optimal subtree as a function of $\alpha$, from 16 to a stump. Right: cross-validated and test accuracy along the path; the dotted line marks the best cross-validated subtree, with 4 leaves.

The best subtree has 4 leaves and depth 3, cross-validated accuracy 0.925 and a test accuracy within one case of the 16-leaf tree; the twelve branches beyond it were fitting noise. This pruned tree is the single tree used in Section 7, and the one whose rules one would show to a clinician.

6.8 Feature importance and its caveats

A tree offers a natural measure of each feature's contribution: the total impurity decrease of all splits on that feature, weighted by node size and normalised to sum to one — the impurity-based importance (mean decrease in impurity, MDI), available as feature_importances_.[7],[24] Strobl and colleagues documented two caveats.[16] It is biased towards features with many split points: a continuous feature offers the greedy search more chances to find a spuriously good split than a binary one, so even a pure-noise continuous feature receives importance. And among correlated features the credit is distributed arbitrarily: whichever near-duplicate is chosen at the root takes it. The cell shows the first bias in pure form — four noise features with different numbers of levels and nothing else — and then both effects on the real data, using a forest (Section 7) to average over the arbitrariness of single trees.

# Caveat 1 of impurity importance: four PURE-NOISE features (no relation with the label) with different numbers of split points.
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
noise = pd.DataFrame({"noise_continuous": rng.normal(size=len(X_tr)),             # hundreds of candidate thresholds
                      "noise_20_levels": rng.integers(0, 20, len(X_tr)),         # 19 candidate thresholds
                      "noise_4_levels":  rng.integers(0, 4, len(X_tr)),          # 3 candidate thresholds
                      "noise_binary":    rng.integers(0, 2, len(X_tr))},         # 1 candidate threshold
                     index=X_tr.index)
rf_null = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300, random_state=0).fit(noise, y_tr)
print("impurity importance when EVERY feature is noise (should be equal if unbiased):")
print(pd.Series(rf_null.feature_importances_, index=noise.columns).round(3).to_string())

# The same noise features added to the real data: still non-zero, and the correlated size features share the credit.
rf_mix = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300, random_state=0).fit(pd.concat([X_tr, noise], axis=1), y_tr)
imp = pd.Series(rf_mix.feature_importances_, index=list(X_tr.columns) + list(noise.columns)).sort_values(ascending=False)
print(f"\nwith the 30 real features: noise_continuous {imp['noise_continuous']:.4f} vs noise_binary {imp['noise_binary']:.4f} "
      f"(ranks {imp.index.get_loc('noise_continuous') + 1} and {imp.index.get_loc('noise_binary') + 1} of {len(imp)})")
size3 = imp[["worst radius", "worst perimeter", "worst area"]]
print(f"the three near-duplicate size features: {size3.round(3).to_dict()} -> group total {size3.sum():.3f}")

impurity importance when EVERY feature is noise (should be equal if unbiased):
noise_continuous    0.570
noise_20_levels     0.289
noise_4_levels      0.100
noise_binary        0.041

with the 30 real features: noise_continuous 0.0021 vs noise_binary 0.0005 (ranks 32 and 34 of 34)
the three near-duplicate size features: {'worst radius': 0.107, 'worst perimeter': 0.163, 'worst area': 0.095} -> group total 0.365

When every feature is noise the importances should be equal; instead they are ordered by the number of candidate thresholds — about 0.57 for the continuous feature against 0.04 for the binary one, with no information in either. Among the 30 real features the noise features rank near the bottom but not at zero, and the three near-duplicate size measurements share a group total of about 0.36 in seed-dependent proportions. The rules: never read impurity importance as causal or marginal relevance; compare it with permutation importance (Section 7.4); report correlated features as a group.[16],[17]

6.9 Regression trees

The same algorithm fits a continuous target. In a regression tree each leaf predicts the mean of the training targets reaching it, the impurity is their variance, and the prediction is piecewise constant: a step function in one dimension. The diabetes data of Unit 2 — 442 patients, ten baseline variables, disease progression after one year[29] — show it.

# A regression tree on the diabetes data: rules, R^2 on the test part, and the step-function fit along body-mass index.
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeRegressor
diab = datasets.load_diabetes(as_frame=True)
Xd, yd = diab.data, diab.target
Xd_tr, Xd_te, yd_tr, yd_te = train_test_split(Xd, yd, test_size=0.3, random_state=0)

reg2 = DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=2, random_state=0).fit(Xd_tr, yd_tr)
reg_full = DecisionTreeRegressor(random_state=0).fit(Xd_tr, yd_tr)
print(export_text(reg2, feature_names=list(Xd.columns), decimals=3))
print(f"depth-2 tree: R^2 on training {reg2.score(Xd_tr, yd_tr):.3f}, on test {reg2.score(Xd_te, yd_te):.3f}")
print(f"unpruned tree ({reg_full.get_n_leaves()} leaves): R^2 on training {reg_full.score(Xd_tr, yd_tr):.3f}, on test {reg_full.score(Xd_te, yd_te):.3f}")

# One-dimensional view: a tree on 'bmi' alone, at two depths, is a step function.
grid = np.linspace(Xd["bmi"].min(), Xd["bmi"].max(), 400).reshape(-1, 1)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.6))
ax.scatter(Xd_tr["bmi"], yd_tr, s=10, color=GREY, alpha=0.6, label="training patients")
for d, col in [(1, ORANGE), (3, BLUE)]:
    r = DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=d, random_state=0).fit(Xd_tr[["bmi"]], yd_tr)
    ax.step(grid.ravel(), r.predict(pd.DataFrame(grid, columns=["bmi"])), where="mid", color=col, lw=1.6, label=f"regression tree on bmi, depth {d} ({r.get_n_leaves()} leaves)")
ax.set_xlabel("body-mass index (standardised units, as distributed with the dataset)"); ax.set_ylabel("disease progression after one year")
ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8); ax.set_title("A regression tree predicts a piecewise-constant function")
fig.tight_layout()

Figure 11. Disease progression against body-mass index for the training patients, with regression trees of depth 1 and depth 3 fitted to this feature alone: constant within each leaf, jumping at each threshold.

The depth-2 tree splits on s5 (a serum measurement) and then on body-mass index and explains a fifth of the variance of the unseen patients ($R^2 = 0.21$); the unpruned tree, with a leaf per training patient, has a negative test $R^2$ — worse than predicting the mean. The step function also shows a limitation: a tree represents a smooth trend only as a staircase and extrapolates as a constant. Forests inherit both, attenuated.

6.10 Strengths and weaknesses of a single tree

Strengths. No feature scaling (Section 6.4); continuous and categorical features in one model, and missing values by surrogate splits or a learned default direction (native in scikit-learn since 1.3); interpretability — the model is a short list of rules and each prediction a path; fast training, $O(p\,n\log n)$ per level, and $O(\text{depth})$ prediction; interactions captured automatically (texture matters only among large tumours in Figure 8).

Weaknesses. Instability: the algorithm is greedy and each split is chosen by a small margin, so a small change in the training data can change the root and everything below it — the property Breiman named when he introduced bagging.[11] And axis-aligned boundaries: an oblique boundary must be approximated by a staircase of many splits. Two cells demonstrate each.

# Weakness 1, instability: two trees grown on two bootstrap samples of the same training data.
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
boots = [rng.integers(0, len(X_tr), len(X_tr)) for _ in range(2)]        # sampling with replacement, same size as the data
for b, idx in enumerate(boots, 1):
    t = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=2, random_state=0).fit(X_tr.iloc[idx], y_tr.iloc[idx])
    print(f"bootstrap sample {b}: {len(np.unique(idx))} distinct training cases of {len(idx)}")
    print(export_text(t, feature_names=list(X.columns), class_names=["malignant", "benign"], decimals=2))
t_a = DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=0).fit(X_tr.iloc[boots[0]], y_tr.iloc[boots[0]])
t_b = DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=0).fit(X_tr.iloc[boots[1]], y_tr.iloc[boots[1]])
disagree = np.mean(t_a.predict(X_te) != t_b.predict(X_te))
print(f"two unpruned trees from the two samples disagree on {disagree:.1%} of the {len(X_te)} test cases")

Each bootstrap sample contains about 63 % of the distinct training cases (Section 7.3 explains the number), so the two samples differ only in which of the same 398 patients are repeated. The two depth-2 trees nevertheless differ in thresholds and in the features below the root, and two unpruned trees from the two samples disagree on about 10 % of the test cases. For a clinical rule this is uncomfortable — the published rule depends on which patients happened to be sampled — and it is the property Section 7 turns into an advantage.

# Weakness 2, axis-aligned boundaries: a tree on two features partitions the plane into rectangles.
feats = ["worst radius", "worst concave points"]
X2_tr, X2_te = X_tr[feats].to_numpy(), X_te[feats].to_numpy()
tree_2d = DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=0).fit(X2_tr, y_tr)
tree_2d_p = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=3, random_state=0).fit(X2_tr, y_tr)
xx, yy = np.meshgrid(np.linspace(7, 37, 300), np.linspace(-0.01, 0.30, 300))
grid2 = np.c_[xx.ravel(), yy.ravel()]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.5, 3.8))
for ax, model, title in [(axes[0], tree_2d_p, f"depth-3 tree ({tree_2d_p.get_n_leaves()} leaves)"),
                         (axes[1], tree_2d, f"unpruned tree ({tree_2d.get_n_leaves()} leaves)")]:
    Z = model.predict(grid2).reshape(xx.shape)
    ax.contourf(xx, yy, Z, levels=[-0.5, 0.5, 1.5], colors=["#fbe3d3", "#dfe7f1"], alpha=0.9)
    for c, col, name in [(0, ORANGE, "malignant"), (1, BLUE, "benign")]:
        ax.scatter(*X2_te[y_te == c].T, color=col, s=12, edgecolor="none", label=f"test, {name}")
    ax.set_xlabel(feats[0]); ax.set_ylabel(feats[1]); ax.set_title(f"{title}: test accuracy {model.score(X2_te, y_te):.3f}")
axes[0].legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8)
fig.tight_layout()

Figure 12. Decision regions of a depth-3 tree (left) and an unpruned tree (right) on two features, with the test cases on top. Every boundary is horizontal or vertical. The unpruned tree carves thin slivers around individual training cases; the depth-3 tree draws a few large boxes and is slightly more accurate on the test cases.

Where the true boundary is oblique — malignancy rises with radius and concave points together — a tree can only approximate it with steps, and the finer the steps the fewer training cases each is fitted to. Compare the smooth boundaries of the SVM and k-NN in Unit 3; forests soften the staircase by averaging many of them.

Exercise 3

Replace feats by ["mean texture", "mean smoothness"], two weak features: how many leaves does the unpruned tree grow, and what is its test accuracy? Then set min_samples_leaf=10 in both trees. How does the picture change, and why is this stopping rule often preferable to a depth limit?

7. Random forests

7.1 Bagging: averaging unstable predictors

In 1996 Breiman proposed a remedy for instability that is almost embarrassingly simple: train many trees, each on a different bootstrap sample ($n$ cases drawn with replacement from the $n$ available), and combine them by vote or average. He called it bagging, for bootstrap aggregating, and showed that it helps unstable predictors substantially while leaving stable ones such as k-NN almost unchanged.[11] The reason is a fact about averages: if $B$ predictors each have variance $\sigma^2$ and pairwise correlation $\rho$,

$$\operatorname{Var}\!\left(\frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B} \hat f_b\right) = \rho\,\sigma^2 + \frac{1-\rho}{B}\,\sigma^2 .$$ The second term vanishes as $B$ grows: averaging removes the independent part of the variability. The first does not: whatever the trees have in common survives.[23]

The cell simulates the formula with $\hat f_b = \sqrt{\rho}\,c + \sqrt{1-\rho}\,e_b$ (shared $c$, independent $e_b$, all standard normal).

# Variance of the average of B predictors with pairwise correlation rho: simulation versus the formula rho + (1 - rho)/B.
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
Bs = np.array([1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 12, 20, 35, 60, 100, 200]); reps = 4000
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.6))
for rho, col in [(0.0, GREEN), (0.25, BLUE), (0.5, ORANGE), (0.75, GREY)]:
    sim = []
    for B in Bs:
        shared = rng.normal(size=(reps, 1)); indiv = rng.normal(size=(reps, B))
        preds = np.sqrt(rho) * shared + np.sqrt(1 - rho) * indiv            # B predictors, each with variance 1, correlation rho
        sim.append(preds.mean(axis=1).var())
    ax.plot(Bs, sim, "o", color=col, ms=4)
    ax.plot(Bs, rho + (1 - rho) / Bs, "-", color=col, lw=1.2, label=f"rho = {rho:.2f}")
ax.set_xscale("log"); ax.set_xlabel("number of averaged predictors B"); ax.set_ylabel("variance of the average")
ax.set_ylim(0, 1.05); ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8, title="pairwise correlation", title_fontsize=8)
ax.set_title("Averaging removes independent variability but not shared variability")
fig.tight_layout()
print("variance of a single predictor: 1.  Floor as B -> infinity: rho.  At B = 200 the simulated variances are:",
      {rho: round(float(v), 3) for rho, v in zip([0.0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75], [rho + (1 - rho) / 200 for rho in [0.0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75]])})

variance of a single predictor: 1.  Floor as B -> infinity: rho.  At B = 200 the simulated variances are: {0.0: 0.005, 0.25: 0.254, 0.5: 0.502, 0.75: 0.751}

Figure 13. Variance of the average of $B$ unit-variance predictors for four pairwise correlations; points simulated, lines the formula. With $\rho = 0$ the variance falls as $1/B$; with $\rho = 0.5$ it reaches a floor of 0.5 after a few dozen predictors.

Trees grown on bootstrap samples of the same data are strongly correlated — they tend to choose the same strong feature at the root — so their errors are shared. To push $\rho$ down one must make the trees more different, even at the cost of making each individually worse.

7.2 Random feature subsets

That is the idea Ho introduced in 1995 as the random subspace method[13],[14] and that Breiman combined with bagging in 2001 to define the random forest:[12] at every node of every tree only a random subset of $m$ of the $p$ features is considered (max_features; by default $m = \sqrt{p}$ for classification). A tree forbidden from using worst perimeter at some node must find the next-best feature, and trees that differ at the root diverge below it. Each tree is somewhat worse; the ensemble is better. Trees are grown to full depth without pruning — their individual overfitting is averaged away — so a forest has essentially two parameters, $m$ and $B$, and is insensitive to both over a wide range. Breiman's bound makes the trade explicit: the generalisation error is at most $\bar\rho\,(1 - s^2)/s^2$, with $\bar\rho$ the mean correlation between trees and $s$ their average strength.[12]

7.3 Out-of-bag error: a free validation estimate

Each bootstrap sample omits on average a fraction $(1 - 1/n)^n \approx e^{-1} \approx 0.368$ of the training cases — the out-of-bag (OOB) cases of that tree. Any training case is thus out of bag for about a third of the trees, which can classify it as if it were new. Comparing the OOB vote for each case with its label gives the OOB error, an estimate of generalisation error without a test set or cross-validation, at no cost; Breiman showed it is about as accurate as a test set of the training set's size.[15],[12] The cell fits 300 trees with oob_score=True and compares OOB, cross-validated and test accuracy.

# A random forest on the training part: out-of-bag accuracy versus cross-validation versus the held-out test set.
n = len(X_tr)
print(f"fraction of cases left out of one bootstrap sample: (1 - 1/{n})^{n} = {(1 - 1/n) ** n:.3f}  (e^-1 = {np.exp(-1):.3f})")

rf = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300, oob_score=True, random_state=0).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
cv_rf = cross_val_score(RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300, random_state=0), X_tr, y_tr, cv=cv5)
oob_votes = rf.oob_decision_function_                               # class probabilities from the OOB trees only
trees_per_case = np.mean([np.isin(np.arange(n), est_idx, invert=True).mean() for est_idx in
                          [rf.estimators_samples_[b] for b in range(rf.n_estimators)]])
print(f"on average each training case is out of bag for {trees_per_case:.1%} of the {rf.n_estimators} trees")
pd.DataFrame({"estimate": ["OOB accuracy (training cases, OOB trees)", "5-fold CV accuracy (training part)",
                           "accuracy on the 171 held-out test cases", "accuracy on the training cases themselves"],
              "value": [rf.oob_score_, cv_rf.mean(), rf.score(X_te, y_te), rf.score(X_tr, y_tr)]}).set_index("estimate").round(3)

fraction of cases left out of one bootstrap sample: (1 - 1/398)^398 = 0.367  (e^-1 = 0.368)
on average each training case is out of bag for 36.7% of the 300 trees
value
estimate
OOB accuracy (training cases, OOB trees) 0.967
5-fold CV accuracy (training part) 0.957
accuracy on the 171 held-out test cases 0.953
accuracy on the training cases themselves 1.000

The OOB estimate (0.967), the cross-validated estimate (0.957) and the test accuracy (0.953) agree to within one and a half percentage points, while the accuracy on the training cases is 1.0, as it must be for unpruned trees, and says nothing. In practice the OOB estimate replaces cross-validation for forests: it costs nothing, uses all the data, and can be monitored as trees are added — which answers "how many trees?".

# OOB error as a function of the number of trees. warm_start=True adds trees to the existing forest instead of refitting.
import warnings
sizes = [5, 10, 15, 20, 30, 50, 75, 100, 150, 200, 300, 400, 500]
rf_grow = RandomForestClassifier(oob_score=True, warm_start=True, random_state=0)
oob_err = []
with warnings.catch_warnings():
    warnings.simplefilter("ignore")                                 # with very few trees some cases have no OOB vote yet
    for B in sizes:
        rf_grow.set_params(n_estimators=B).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
        oob_err.append(1 - rf_grow.oob_score_)
single_err = 1 - cross_val_score(DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=0), X_tr, y_tr, cv=cv5).mean()

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.4))
ax.plot(sizes, oob_err, "o-", color=BLUE, label="OOB error of the forest")
ax.axhline(single_err, color=ORANGE, ls="--", label=f"single unpruned tree (5-fold CV error {single_err:.3f})")
ax.set_xscale("log"); ax.set_xlabel("number of trees B"); ax.set_ylabel("error rate"); ax.set_ylim(0, max(oob_err) * 1.1)
ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8); ax.set_title("Out-of-bag error versus number of trees")
fig.tight_layout()
print(f"single unpruned tree, 5-fold CV error: {single_err:.3f}")
print("OOB error by number of trees:", {B: round(e, 3) for B, e in zip(sizes, oob_err)})

single unpruned tree, 5-fold CV error: 0.083
OOB error by number of trees: {5: 0.126, 10: 0.058, 15: 0.055, 20: 0.048, 30: 0.038, 50: 0.04, 75: 0.033, 100: 0.03, 150: 0.033, 200: 0.03, 300: 0.033, 400: 0.035, 500: 0.035}

Figure 14. Out-of-bag error as trees are added, against the cross-validated error of a single unpruned tree (dashed, 0.083). The forest's error falls steeply over the first few dozen trees and plateaus at 0.03–0.035 from about a hundred — less than half the single tree's error.

With very few trees many cases have only one or two OOB votes and the estimate is noisy; by 50 to 100 trees it has reached its plateau, and 300 to 500 is a safe default at this size. The number of trees cannot be over-fitted: more trees never increase the expected error, only the time.

7.4 Feature importance: impurity-based versus permutation

A forest inherits the impurity importance of Section 6.8, averaged over trees, and offers a second measure: permutation importance. Randomly permute one feature's values among the evaluation cases — destroying its relation with the label while keeping its distribution — and measure the drop in accuracy. A feature the model does not use gives a drop of zero whatever its number of split points, which removes the first bias of Section 6.8.[12],[16] Correlation remains: if worst radius is permuted but worst perimeter is intact, the forest keeps almost the same information and the drop is small for each member of a correlated group even when the group is essential; conditional permutation and corrected permutation tests address this.[17],[18] The cell computes both measures for the 300-tree forest, permutation importance on the test cases with ten repetitions.

# Impurity-based importance versus permutation importance (on the test cases) for the same forest. They disagree.
from sklearn.inspection import permutation_importance
perm = permutation_importance(rf, X_te, y_te, n_repeats=10, random_state=0)
imp_df = pd.DataFrame({"impurity (MDI)": rf.feature_importances_, "permutation (test, mean drop in accuracy)": perm.importances_mean,
                       "permutation std": perm.importances_std}, index=X.columns)
top = imp_df.sort_values("impurity (MDI)", ascending=False).head(12)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.5, 4), sharey=True)
axes[0].barh(top.index[::-1], top["impurity (MDI)"][::-1], color=BLUE); axes[0].set_title("impurity-based importance (sums to 1)")
axes[1].barh(top.index[::-1], top["permutation (test, mean drop in accuracy)"][::-1], xerr=top["permutation std"][::-1], color=ORANGE, capsize=2)
axes[1].set_title("permutation importance (drop in test accuracy)")
axes[0].set_xlabel("mean decrease in impurity"); axes[1].set_xlabel("decrease in accuracy when permuted")
fig.suptitle("Twelve features with the highest impurity importance, under both measures", fontsize=10, fontweight="bold")
fig.tight_layout()
print(f"sum of impurity importances of the 12 features shown: {top['impurity (MDI)'].sum():.2f}")
print(f"largest single permutation drop: {imp_df['permutation (test, mean drop in accuracy)'].max():.3f} "
      f"({imp_df['permutation (test, mean drop in accuracy)'].idxmax()}); features whose permutation drop is <= 0: "
      f"{(imp_df['permutation (test, mean drop in accuracy)'] <= 0).sum()} of 30")

sum of impurity importances of the 12 features shown: 0.86
largest single permutation drop: 0.021 (worst radius); features whose permutation drop is <= 0: 15 of 30

Figure 15. Left: impurity importance of the twelve highest-ranked features (together 0.86 of the total). Right: permutation importance of the same features on the test cases, with the standard deviation over ten permutations. The orderings differ — worst radius and worst area overtake worst perimeter — and every drop is small: no single feature, scrambled, costs more than about two percentage points, and half of the 30 features cost nothing.

Impurity importance says "these features were used a lot"; permutation importance says "the predictions depend on this feature given that the others are available". With near-duplicate size measurements the first is spread over the group and the second is small for every member. Neither says "this feature causes malignancy". For a per-patient explanation the modern tool is the Shapley-value decomposition for trees, beyond this unit.[31]

7.5 Partial dependence: what does the forest do with a feature?

A forest has no coefficients, but one can ask how its prediction changes, on average, when one feature is varied with the others left as observed — the partial dependence on feature $j$ at value $v$:[19]

$$\overline{f}_j(v) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \hat f\big(x_{i1}, \dots, x_{i,j-1},\, v,\, x_{i,j+1}, \dots, x_{ip}\big),$$ computed below directly from the definition for the two features of Figure 12 (scikit-learn provides PartialDependenceDisplay).
# Partial dependence of the forest's predicted probability of malignancy on two features, computed from the definition.
def partial_dependence(model, Xdf, feature, grid):
    '''Average predicted P(malignant) when `feature` is set to each grid value for every training case.'''
    out = []
    for v in grid:
        Xv = Xdf.copy(); Xv[feature] = v
        out.append(model.predict_proba(Xv)[:, 0].mean())        # column 0 = malignant
    return np.array(out)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.5, 3.4))
for ax, f in zip(axes, ["worst radius", "worst concave points"]):
    grid = np.quantile(X_tr[f], np.linspace(0.02, 0.98, 40))
    pd_curve = partial_dependence(rf, X_tr, f, grid)
    ax.plot(grid, pd_curve, color=BLUE, lw=1.8)
    ax.plot(X_tr[f], np.full(len(X_tr), 0.29), "|", color=GREY, alpha=0.4)   # rug: where the training data are
    ax.set_xlabel(f); ax.set_ylabel("mean predicted P(malignant)"); ax.set_ylim(0.28, 0.56); ax.set_title(f"partial dependence on '{f}'")
    print(f"{f}: P(malignant) rises from {pd_curve[0]:.2f} at {grid[0]:.3f} to {pd_curve[-1]:.2f} at {grid[-1]:.3f}")
fig.tight_layout()

worst radius: P(malignant) rises from 0.33 at 9.472 to 0.50 at 28.249
worst concave points: P(malignant) rises from 0.33 at 0.009 to 0.46 at 0.263

Figure 16. Partial dependence of the forest's predicted probability of malignancy on worst radius and worst concave points; ticks mark the training values. Both curves rise over a narrow range — where the trees place most thresholds — and are flat outside it: a smooth version of the step functions of Section 6.9, because hundreds of steps at slightly different thresholds average to a ramp.

The curves rise from about 0.33 to 0.50 and 0.46, not to 1: setting one feature to a malignant-looking value does not change the prediction for a patient whose other 29 features look benign — which is also the caution: such combinations may never occur in the data. Even so, a partial-dependence curve shows direction, shape and the range over which a feature matters, which no importance score does.

7.6 The forest against the single tree and the methods of Unit 3

The last experiment compares, under the S1 protocol, the pruned tree of Section 6.7, the forest, and the three classifiers of Unit 3 — Gaussian naive Bayes, k-nearest neighbours and the RBF-kernel SVM, the latter two with standardisation in a pipeline — by stratified 5-fold cross-validation repeated three times on the training part (accuracy and ROC AUC) and once on the test part.

# Comparison under the S1 protocol: repeated stratified CV on the training part (accuracy, ROC AUC), then one test-set evaluation.
from sklearn.model_selection import RepeatedStratifiedKFold, cross_validate
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.naive_bayes import GaussianNB
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier
from sklearn.svm import SVC

models = {
    "decision tree, pruned (Sec. 6.7)": DecisionTreeClassifier(ccp_alpha=best["ccp_alpha"], random_state=0),
    "random forest, 300 trees":          RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300, random_state=0),
    "Gaussian naive Bayes (Unit 3)":     GaussianNB(),
    "k-NN, k=5, standardised (Unit 3)":  make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=5)),
    "SVM, RBF kernel, standardised (Unit 3)": make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), SVC(random_state=0)),
}
rcv = RepeatedStratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, n_repeats=3, random_state=0)
rows = []
for name, m in models.items():
    res = cross_validate(m, X_tr, y_tr, cv=rcv, scoring=["accuracy", "roc_auc"])
    m.fit(X_tr, y_tr)
    rows.append({"model": name, "CV accuracy": res["test_accuracy"].mean(), "CV acc. std": res["test_accuracy"].std(),
                 "CV ROC AUC": res["test_roc_auc"].mean(), "test accuracy": m.score(X_te, y_te)})
comparison = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("model")
comparison.round(3)
CV accuracy CV acc. std CV ROC AUC test accuracy
model
decision tree, pruned (Sec. 6.7) 0.929 0.023 0.931 0.901
random forest, 300 trees 0.962 0.019 0.995 0.953
Gaussian naive Bayes (Unit 3) 0.943 0.013 0.992 0.924
k-NN, k=5, standardised (Unit 3) 0.969 0.020 0.993 0.947
SVM, RBF kernel, standardised (Unit 3) 0.982 0.014 0.995 0.953

The forest improves on the pruned tree by about three points of cross-validated accuracy and six points of ROC AUC (0.995 against 0.931): averaging unstable trees pays. Among the strong methods the standardised SVM is best here (0.982), with k-NN (0.969) and the forest (0.962) within about one standard deviation of each other; naive Bayes is a little lower and the single tree clearly last. The picture is representative: in a comparison of 179 classifiers on 121 datasets, random forests were the family most often best or near-best, with SVMs close behind,[22] and recent benchmarks on medium-sized tabular data still find tree ensembles ahead of deep neural networks.[21],[32] What the forest offers that the SVM does not is the absence of scaling, mixed feature types, a free error estimate, and importance and partial-dependence tools; what it gives up relative to the single tree is the readable rule list — the trade Breiman described in his essay on the "two cultures" of statistical modelling.[30]

# The forest's decision regions on the two features of Figure 12, next to the unpruned tree's.
rf_2d = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300, random_state=0).fit(X2_tr, y_tr)
