fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.5, 3.8))
for ax, model, title in [(axes[0], tree_2d, "unpruned tree"), (axes[1], rf_2d, "random forest (300 trees)")]:

    cf = ax.contourf(xx, yy, P, levels=np.linspace(0, 1, 11), cmap="RdBu_r", alpha=0.85)

        ax.scatter(*X2_te[y_te == c].T, color=col, s=12, edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.3, label=f"test, {name}")
    ax.set_xlabel(feats[0]); ax.set_ylabel(feats[1]); ax.set_title(f"{title}, test accuracy {model.score(X2_te, y_te):.3f}", fontsize=9)

Figure 17. Predicted probability of malignancy over the plane of two features, for the unpruned tree (left) and the forest (right); the black line is the 0.5 contour. The tree's probabilities are 0 or 1 everywhere, with rectangular islands around individual training cases; the forest's grade smoothly, the islands are averaged away, and test accuracy rises from 0.912 to 0.936.

Averaging a few hundred staircases produces a smoother boundary and graded uncertainty: the pale region near the boundary is where the trees disagree, and a clinician should read a probability of 0.55 differently from one of 0.98.

Random forests in one paragraph

Grow $B$ unpruned trees, each on a bootstrap sample, considering at each node only $m \approx \sqrt{p}$ random features; predict by vote or average. Bootstrap and feature subsampling decorrelate the trees so that averaging reduces variance (Figure 13); the out-of-bag cases estimate the error for free (Section 7.3); $B$ need only reach the plateau (Figure 14); the price is the loss of a single readable tree, partly compensated by importance measures and partial dependence.

8. Beyond the plan: gradient boosting

Not in the official syllabus

This section goes one step beyond the unit because the method is, in current practice, the default for tabular data, and because it is the natural counterpart of the forest: both are tree ensembles that combine their trees in opposite ways.

A forest grows its trees independently and averages them to reduce variance. Gradient boosting, formulated by Friedman in 2001, grows shallow trees sequentially, each fitted to the negative gradient of the loss of the ensemble so far, and adds them with a small learning rate, reducing bias step by step.[19] XGBoost (2016) made the method fast and regularised, and it and its successors — LightGBM, CatBoost, scikit-learn's HistGradientBoostingClassifier, which bins each feature into at most 255 values to speed up the threshold scan of Section 6.4 — have won most competitions on tabular data since.[20] Systematic comparisons find boosted trees and forests still ahead of deep networks on medium-sized tables, apparently because tree ensembles ignore uninformative features and represent irregular functions that networks smooth over.[21],[32] Unlike a forest, boosting can overfit as trees are added, so their number must be chosen by validation or early stopping.

# Gradient boosting (histogram-based) added to the comparison of Section 7.6, same protocol.
from sklearn.ensemble import HistGradientBoostingClassifier
hgb = HistGradientBoostingClassifier(max_iter=200, learning_rate=0.05, max_depth=3, random_state=0)
res = cross_validate(hgb, X_tr, y_tr, cv=rcv, scoring=["accuracy", "roc_auc"])
hgb.fit(X_tr, y_tr)
comparison.loc["gradient boosting, 200 depth-3 trees (Sec. 8)"] = [res["test_accuracy"].mean(), res["test_accuracy"].std(),
                                                                   res["test_roc_auc"].mean(), hgb.score(X_te, y_te)]
comparison.round(3)

Boosting lands in the same group as the forest and the SVM, within fold-to-fold noise on these 398 training cases. On larger, messier tables — many uninformative features, missing values, mixed types — the gap between tree ensembles and the methods of Unit 3 usually widens in favour of the ensembles; on small, clean problems a tuned SVM is often as good and easier to defend. The comparison should be run under the S1 protocol, not assumed.

9. Applications in medicine and bioengineering

Decision trees entered medicine before they entered machine learning, because a clinician's protocol is a tree.

Triage of chest pain (1982). Goldman and colleagues applied recursive partitioning — CART, with Olshen among the authors — to 482 emergency-room patients to derive a protocol predicting myocardial infarction from the electrocardiogram and history; tested prospectively on 468 further patients, the protocol combined with physicians' judgement kept sensitivity while raising the specificity of intensive-care admission from 67 % to 77 %.[27] The CART monograph, published two years later, opens with medical examples from the same period, including the prognosis of heart-attack patients at the University of California, San Diego.[7] The protocol could be printed on a card and used at the bedside.

Clinical decision rules (1992). The Ottawa ankle rules, derived by Stiell and colleagues from 750 patients, are a sequence of yes/no questions on bone tenderness and the ability to bear weight that identifies patients who need no radiograph — operationally a shallow decision tree executed by hand; in the derivation study they had 100 % sensitivity for fracture.[26] Most decision rules in emergency medicine have this form because a tree can be memorised and applied under time pressure: the interpretability of Section 6.10 is what makes them usable.

Genomics (2006). With thousands of features and tens of patients — gene-expression microarrays — single trees are hopeless and most methods of Unit 3 need heavy feature selection. Díaz-Uriarte and Alvarez de Andrés showed that random forests classify such data as well as the best alternatives without pre-selection, and proposed gene selection by iteratively discarding the least important genes while monitoring the OOB error.[25] The biases of importance measures (Sections 6.8 and 7.4) were documented precisely because of their use for gene ranking.[16],[18]

Reading a tree-based paper

Was the tree pruned, and how was the depth or $\alpha$ chosen — on the test data? Is the reported accuracy OOB, cross-validated or on an independent set? If importances are interpreted, are the features correlated, and was permutation importance used? Are the rules plausible to a clinician, or do they suggest shortcut learning (Unit 1, Section 7.3)?

10. Summary

You should now be able to explain, without notes:

  • The recursive definition of a binary tree and its vocabulary (root, leaf, depth, height in edges with −1 for the empty tree; full, perfect, complete).
  • The three representations; that scikit-learn stores a tree as arrays indexed by node.
  • The four traversals; that pre-order prints a tree as rules and in-order yields a search tree's keys in sorted order.
  • That a perfect tree of height $h$ has $2^{h+1}-1$ nodes, so the height of an $n$-node tree lies between $\log_2(n+1)-1$ and $n-1$.
  • The BST invariant; insertion and search in $O(h)$; deletion via the in-order successor; sorted insertion gives $h = n-1$, random insertion $h \propto \log n$.
  • What a rotation does; what AVL, red–black and B-trees guarantee and where they are used.
  • Gini, entropy and misclassification, and why the concave ones are used for growing; the greedy CART algorithm and the threshold scan; why trees need no scaling.
  • Depth versus overfitting; cost-complexity pruning; the two biases of impurity importance; regression trees as piecewise-constant functions; instability and axis-aligned boundaries.
  • Bagging and $\rho\sigma^2 + (1-\rho)\sigma^2/B$; random feature subsets as the way to reduce $\rho$; the OOB estimate and $e^{-1}$; impurity versus permutation importance; partial dependence; how the forest compares with a single tree and with Unit 3.

11. Self-assessment

1. A binary tree has 20 nodes. What are the minimum and maximum possible heights, and what shapes achieve them?Minimum $\lceil \log_2 21 \rceil - 1 = 4$ (a complete tree: 15 nodes in the first four levels, 5 in the fifth). Maximum 19 (a chain).
2. Give the pre-, in- and post-order traversals of the tree with root 8, left child 3 (children 1 and 6), right child 10 (right child 14 only). Is it a BST?Pre-order 8 3 1 6 10 14; in-order 1 3 6 8 10 14; post-order 1 6 3 14 10 8. Yes: the in-order sequence is strictly increasing.
3. In the array representation a node is stored at index 12. Where are its parent and its children?Parent at $\lfloor 11/2 \rfloor = 5$; children at 25 and 26.
4. Why does inserting patient records into a BST by increasing admission date produce a slow structure, and what are two remedies?Increasing keys always go right, giving a chain of height $n-1$ and $O(n)$ search. Remedies: a self-balancing tree (AVL, red–black, B-tree), or median-first insertion if all keys are known in advance.
5. A right rotation is applied at y with left child x. Which subtree changes parent, and why is the in-order sequence unchanged?The right subtree of x (keys between x and y) becomes the left subtree of y; in-order before and after is (left of x), x, (that subtree), y, (right of y).
6. A node has 8 malignant and 2 benign cases. Compute Gini and entropy. A split sends the 2 benign and 2 malignant left and 6 malignant right: compute the decrease in Gini.Gini $= 1 - (0.64 + 0.04) = 0.32$; entropy $\approx 0.722$ bits. Left: Gini 0.5; right: 0. Weighted $0.4 \times 0.5 = 0.2$; decrease $0.12$.
7. Why do CART and C4.5 grow trees with Gini or entropy rather than with the misclassification error that is finally reported?Gini and entropy are strictly concave, so any split that makes the children purer decreases them even without changing a majority class; the piecewise-linear misclassification error can remain unchanged under a useful split and would stop growth prematurely.
8. In Section 6.4 the stump on 'worst radius' and the exhaustive scan agreed, but the stump on all 30 features chose 'worst perimeter'. What does this say about the stability of the root split?The choice between near-duplicate features is decided by a small difference in weighted Gini, hence by a few training cases. A bootstrap sample can flip it, and because every lower split depends on the root the whole tree changes — the instability bagging exploits.
9. Code reading: a colleague selects max_depth from the orange test-accuracy curve of Figure 9 instead of the blue one. What is wrong?The test set has been used for model selection, so its accuracy at the chosen depth is optimistically biased. Choose depth by cross-validation (or OOB) on the training part and evaluate the test set once, at the end.
10. Explain in one sentence each what bagging and random feature subsets do to $\rho\sigma^2 + (1-\rho)\sigma^2/B$.Bagging increases $B$, shrinking the second term; random feature subsets decrease $\rho$ by making trees choose different splits, lowering the floor, at the cost of a somewhat larger $\sigma^2$ per tree.
11. With 398 training cases and 300 trees, roughly how many trees have a given case out of bag, and why does the OOB estimate need no separate test set?About $0.368 \times 300 \approx 110$. Those trees never saw the case, so their vote is a prediction on unseen data; aggregated over all cases, the votes estimate the generalisation error.
12. In Figure 15 'worst perimeter' has the highest impurity importance, yet permuting it costs the forest only about 1.5 percentage points. Give the mechanism, and what you would tell a clinician who asks which measurement matters most.Impurity importance credits the feature chosen at many splits; permutation measures the loss when it is scrambled while 'worst radius' and 'worst area', which carry the same information, remain available. Report the correlated size measurements as a group, say that the ranking within it is arbitrary, and show partial-dependence curves rather than a single number.

Glossary

AVL tree
Self-balancing BST in which the subtree heights at every node differ by at most one; height at most about $1.44\log_2 n$.
Bagging
Bootstrap aggregating: training predictors on bootstrap samples and combining them by vote or average to reduce variance.
Binary search tree (BST)
Binary tree of keys in which, at every node, all left keys are smaller and all right keys larger than the node's key.
Binary tree
Rooted tree with at most two children per node, distinguished as left and right; recursively, empty or a root with two binary subtrees.
Bootstrap sample
$n$ cases drawn with replacement from $n$; omits about 36.8 % of the distinct cases.
B-tree
Balanced search tree with many keys per node, designed for disk; the basis of database indexes.
CART
Classification and Regression Trees: greedy recursive partitioning with Gini impurity and cost-complexity pruning; scikit-learn's algorithm.
Cost-complexity pruning
Choosing the subtree minimising training error plus $\alpha$ times the number of leaves, with $\alpha$ selected by cross-validation.
Decision tree
Binary tree whose internal nodes test a feature against a threshold and whose leaves hold a class or value; its decision regions are axis-aligned boxes.
Depth / height
Depth of a node: edges from the root. Height: edges on the longest downward path to a leaf; the tree's height is its root's (−1 if empty).
Entropy / Gini impurity
$-\sum_k p_k\log_2 p_k$ (ID3/C4.5) and $1 - \sum_k p_k^2$ (CART): the impurity measures whose decrease selects a split.
Gradient boosting
Ensemble that adds shallow trees sequentially, each fitted to the gradient of the loss so far; reduces bias.
Impurity-based (MDI) importance
Total impurity decrease attributable to a feature, normalised; biased towards features with many split points and arbitrary among correlated features.
Out-of-bag (OOB) error
Error of a forest on each training case as predicted by the trees whose bootstrap sample excluded it.
Partial dependence
Average prediction as a function of one feature with the others held at their observed values.
Permutation importance
Decrease in performance when one feature's values are randomly permuted.
Random forest
Bagged unpruned trees in which each split considers a random subset of the features.
Red–black tree
Self-balancing BST with a colour bit per node bounding the height by $2\log_2(n+1)$.
Rotation
Local rearrangement of a node and one child that changes subtree heights by one while preserving the in-order sequence.
Traversal
Visiting every node once: pre-order (root first), in-order (root between subtrees), post-order (root last), level-order (by depth).

Textbooks

  • Cormen TH, Leiserson CE, Rivest RL, Stein C. Introduction to Algorithms. 4th ed. MIT Press; 2022. — Chapters 12 (binary search trees) and 13 (red–black trees) for a full treatment, with deletion and rotations, of Sections 2–4.
  • Hastie T, Tibshirani R, Friedman J. The Elements of Statistical Learning. 2nd ed. Springer; 2009. — Chapter 9.2 for CART, Chapter 10 for boosting, Chapter 15 for random forests; the source of the variance formula of Section 7.1. Free PDF from the authors' site.
  • James G, Witten D, Hastie T, Tibshirani R, Taylor J. An Introduction to Statistical Learning with Applications in Python. Springer; 2023. — Chapter 8, tree-based methods: the most accessible treatment of Sections 6–8. Free PDF at statlearning.com.
  • Géron A. Hands-On Machine Learning with Scikit-Learn, Keras and TensorFlow. 3rd ed. O'Reilly; 2022. — Chapters 6 (decision trees) and 7 (ensembles) for the scikit-learn practice.
  • Murphy KP. Probabilistic Machine Learning: An Introduction. MIT Press; 2022. — Chapter 18, trees, forests, bagging and boosting. Free PDF at probml.github.io.
  • Bishop CM. Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning. Springer; 2006. — Section 14.4, tree-based models, for the probabilistic view.

Online resources

  • scikit-learn user guide, "Decision Trees" and "Ensembles: gradient boosting, random forests, bagging" — scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/tree.html and …/ensemble.html; includes the mathematical formulation of CART and the pruning path used in Section 6.7.
  • scikit-learn example, "Understanding the decision tree structure" — scikit-learn.org; walks through the tree_ arrays of Section 6.1.
  • Breiman L, Cutler A. Random Forests — stat.berkeley.edu/~breiman/RandomForests; Breiman's own description of the algorithm, the OOB estimate and the importance measures.
  • Interactive visualisations of binary search trees, AVL and red–black trees (University of San Francisco, D. Galles) — cs.usfca.edu/~galles/visualization; useful to watch rotations happen.
  • UCI Machine Learning Repository — archive.ics.uci.edu; original source of the breast-cancer data.
